agent_notes: Superscription and first verse are one Hebrew verse (KJV 11:0 and 11:1). The Qere נוּדִי (fem. sing. 'flee, you') is glossed; the Ketiv נוּדוּ is plural ('flee, you all'). Rashi and Radak read both, so the note records the written form.

הַרְכֶם צִפּוֹר has no 'as': 'flee, [to] your mountain, [O] bird'. KJV, ASV and Webster supply 'as a bird'; YLT reads it differently ('for the bird'). Ibn Ezra and Radak say a kaf is missing (like 'a lion's whelp Judah'). I kept the bare apposition in the literal layer and the simile in the dramatic one. The word הרכם is also read as 'mountain-ward' (Radak: like 'from your mountain').

[consider] List Radak among the sources for 'in secret', and cite Metzudat Zion for 'darkness'. (PS.11.2 Metzudat Zion: "אופל. חשך"; Radak: "לירות במו אפל כלומר בהסתר")

agent_notes: הַשָּׁתוֹת is rare. Foundations is the usual reading, and Ibn Ezra and Radak also give 'nets/traps'. I took 'foundations' with 'torn down' (הָרַס is used of walls and structures). The perfect פָּעָל is rendered 'what has he done / accomplished', because the five versions split between 'can do' and 'has done'.

Radak and Metzudat Zion use Isa 19:10 for 'foundations'. (PS.11.3 Ibn Ezra: "כי השתות - מצודות, כמו: והיו שתותיה מדוכאים. ויש אומרים: יסודות, כמו וחשופי שת")

agent_notes: The subject of שָׂנְאָה נַפְשׁוֹ is YHWH's own 'soul' (feminine verb with נפש). KJV 'his soul hateth' is ambiguous. Rashi and Radak both take it as God's own soul, but differ on the sense: Rashi, that God hates the wicked and stores up their reward; Radak, that God's soul refuses to reprove them, since they would not accept it, and lets them be until their time comes. I kept the literal verb 'hates' and put Radak's reading in the note.

history.note: [should_fix] In the note on שָׂנְאָה נַפְשׁוֹ, give Radak's reading correctly: God's soul hates (refuses) to reprove the wicked, who would not accept reproof, and he lets them be until their time comes. Do not present it as a reading in which the wicked is the subject. (PS.11.5 Radak: "אבל הרשע ואהב חמס שנאה נפשו מלהוכיח, כי לא יקבל תוכחות עד בא עתו")

[consider] Say that the objects stand first and the line ends on 'his soul' (the subject), and drop 'the verb comes last' in both places. (PS.11.5: "וְרָשָׁע וְאֹהֵב חָמָס שָׂנְאָה נַפְשׁוֹ" (verb at pos 7, subject at pos 8))

agent_notes: פַּחִים 'snares' is retained, with Rashi's 'coals' (פחמים) and Ibn Ezra's 'plates' (Num 17:3, רקועי פחים) as alternatives noted in the commentary. זִלְעָפוֹת: 'burning heat/raging', with Radak's trembling as an alternative, from Ps 119:53 and Lam 5:10. I give 'scorching wind' in the dramatic layer.

agent_notes: יֶחֱזוּ is plural and פָנֵימוֹ has the archaic -מוֹ suffix, which Ibn Ezra, Radak and Meiri read as simply 'his face' (like עלימו). The literal layer shows the plural. The subject of 'see' is ambiguous: 'the upright' may be the subject or the object, and Radak lists both. The dramatic layer takes the upright to see his face, as ASV and BBE do.
